summary: Specifies a "simple mode" for sending facsimile data using Internet mail, using standard protocols and file formats such as MIME and TIFF. It can send to Internet-aware fax devices and other mail recipients, and extensions are to follow.

plainLanguage.summary: To send a fax by email, the image is put in an ordinary mail message as a TIFF file, and a gateway takes it from there: it dials the telephone number and sends the image to the fax machine exactly as a fax machine would. The document defines the message format, the way a fax number is written into the address, what happens when delivery fails, and the extra security questions that arise from joining email and the telephone network.

questions: how to send a fax by email
what image format does internet fax use
subtitle: How a fax page travels as an ordinary email message, and what a gateway has to do to print it on a real fax machine.

tldr.problem: Fax machines speak a compressed image over the telephone network, and email speaks a different protocol entirely. A user who wants to send a fax by email needs both to work together without either side changing.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a profile of ordinary Internet mail: the fax image is carried as a TIFF file in a MIME message, sent with the usual mail protocols, and a gateway called an offramp dials the telephone number and sends the image to the fax machine.
tldr.outcome: The document fixes the message format, the addressing rules for a fax number, and the error handling, and it works through the extra security questions that come from joining two services. It is a revision of RFC 2305 with no technical changes.

facts.label: Image format used
facts.value: TIFF for Facsimile, the S profile

today: RFC 3965 is a Draft Standard published in December 2004 and has not been obsoleted. It is a revision of RFC 2305 with no technical changes, and it builds on the file format defined in RFC 3949. The document says that extensions to it will follow.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This specification defines message-based facsimile communication over the Internet. It describes a minimum set of capabilities, taking into account those of typical facsimile devices and PCs that can generate facsimile data. A G3Fax device is a facsimile-capable device that uses T.4 and the general switched telephone network, and an IFax device is an Internet-accessible device capable of sending, receiving or forwarding Internet faxes. A message can be sent to an IFax device using an Internet mail address, and a message can be sent to a G3Fax device using an Internet mail address, in which case the message may be forwarded through an IFax offramp gateway.

The document defines a profile for Internet mail rather than a distinct service of its own. The semantics that result are designed to be compatible with facsimile operation over the telephone network, so that gateways between facsimile and Internet mail can operate with very high fidelity.

The reason for developing the capability as an email profile is to permit interworking between fax and email users. It is intended that existing email users be able to send ordinary messages to lists of users, including fax recipients, and that other email recipients be able to reply to the original and keep the fax recipients included. Existing email software is expected to work without modification and without having to process new or different data structures beyond what is normal for mail users, and existing mail service standards are used rather than replicating mechanisms more tailored to fax, so that compatibility with the existing mail service is kept.

The specification provides for communication between five combinations: Internet mail to a network printer, Internet mail to an offramp gateway that forwards to a G3Fax device, a network scanner to a network printer, a network scanner to an offramp gateway that forwards to a G3Fax device, and a network scanner to Internet mail.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of doing this as mail rather than as a new service is that everyone already has the software. A person can send a normal email to a fax number, and a reply can go to the same list. Nothing on the mail side has to change, so existing mail programs keep working and the telephone network keeps behaving the way fax machines expect.

sections.title: Transport and Gateways
sections.content:
Data transfer may be achieved using standard Internet mail transfer mechanisms, and the format of addresses must conform to the RFC 821 addr-spec and RFC 822 mailbox standards.

A gateway translates between dissimilar environments, and for IFax a gateway connects between Internet mail and the T.4 telephone facsimile. A gateway may service many facsimile users, in which case it acts as a classic mail transfer agent, or only one, in which case it acts as a classic mail user agent. An onramp is a gateway that connects from the telephone facsimile to Internet mail, and an offramp is a gateway that connects from Internet mail to the telephone facsimile. The behaviour of onramps is out of scope for this specification, which describes the Internet mail service portion of offramp addressing, confirmation and failure notification.

An offramp gateway that operates as a mail transfer agent serving many users should use SMTP, while a gateway that operates as a mail user agent serving a single mail recipient may use a mailbox access protocol such as POP or a similar protocol. The document notes that an offramp gateway that relays mail based on addressing information needs to use the addresses supplied in the MTA envelope rather than addresses listed in the message content headers.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway comes in two kinds. An onramp takes a fax that arrives over the telephone and turns it into mail; the document leaves that alone. An offramp takes mail and dials out to a fax machine, and that is where the addressing, the confirmation and the failure notices are handled. A gateway serving many fax users behaves like a mail server, and one serving a single user may instead pick the mail up from a mailbox.

sections.title: Headers, MIME and the Image
sections.content:
IFax devices must be compliant with the mail header format of RFC 2822 and RFC 1123. The header of an IFax message should include Message-ID and must include all the fields those documents require, such as DATE and FROM. IFax devices must also be compliant with MIME, except as noted in the document's appendix.

The data format of the facsimile image is based on the minimum set of TIFF for Facsimile, also known as the S profile, and such facsimile data are included in a MIME object by use of the image/TIFF sub-type. Additional rules for the use of TIFF for Facsimile in this message-based application are defined later in the document.

A single multi-page document should be sent as a single multi-page TIFF file, even though recipients must process multipart/mixed containing multiple TIFF files. If multipart content is present and the processing of any part fails, then the processing of the whole message is treated as having failed.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is an ordinary mail message with the usual headers, and the page is attached as a TIFF file, in the simplest black-and-white format a fax can use. Sending several pages as one multi-page file is better, but a receiver has to cope with a message that carries several separate files, and if one of them cannot be handled the whole message counts as failed.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
For a delivery failure, the document describes existing requirements for Internet mail rather than special requirements for IFax devices. In the event of a relay failure the sending relay must generate a failure message, which should be in the format of a delivery status notification. Internet mail transported via SMTP must contain a MAIL FROM address appropriate for the delivery of return notices.

A processing failure is a different matter. An IFax device with limited capabilities might be unable to process the content of a message, and in that case it is important that the message is not lost without any notice. Notice may be provided in any appropriate fashion and the exact handling is a local matter.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of failure. If the mail cannot be relayed, the mail system reports it in the usual way, as a delivery status notification. If the mail arrives but the device cannot handle what is inside it, the device should at least let somebody know, because otherwise the message disappears quietly.

sections.title: Addressing
sections.content:
Messages sent to ordinary mail recipients use standard Internet mail addresses, with no additional constraints.

G3Fax devices are accessed through an IFax offramp gateway, which performs any authorized telephone dial-up. When a G3Fax device is identified by a telephone number, the entire address used for that device, including the number and the offramp host reference, must be contained within standard Internet mail transport fields such as RCPT TO and MAIL FROM. The address may also be contained in message content fields, such as the recipient and destination fields, as appropriate.

As for all Internet mail addresses, the left-hand side of an address is not to be interpreted except by the MTA named on the right-hand side, the domain. The telephone number format should conform to the minimal GSTN and fax address formats, and other formats must be syntactically distinct from them.
sections.plainLanguage: An ordinary recipient is addressed in the ordinary way. A fax machine is addressed by its telephone number, together with a reference to the gateway that should dial it, and the whole thing has to sit in the envelope of the mail message rather than only in a header, so that the mail server can act on it.

sections.title: Image File Format
sections.content:
Sending IFax devices must be able to write minimum set TIFF files, following the rules for creating minimum set TIFF files defined in TIFF for Facsimile, the S profile, which is also compatible with the specification for the minimum subset of TIFF-F. Receiving IFax devices must be able to read minimum set TIFF files.

A sender should not use TIFF fields and values beyond the minimum subset of TIFF for Facsimile unless the sender has prior knowledge of other TIFF fields or values supported by the recipient. The mechanism for determining the capabilities of recipients is beyond the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Every sender must be able to write the simplest black-and-white TIFF and every receiver must be able to read it, because that is the common denominator between a fax machine and an email program. Sending anything richer needs prior knowledge that the receiver can handle it, and the document does not define how to find that out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The general directive is that this specification is based on the use of existing Internet mail, so to keep interoperability with mail, any security provided should be part of the Internet security infrastructure rather than a new mechanism outside it.

The document then works through the additional threats that come from joining the two services. A spoofed sender is possible, because the actual sender of the message might not be the one named in the Sender or From headers or in the SMTP envelope, and SMTP implementations do not provide inherent authentication of senders. The usual solution is encryption-based authentication, either for the channel or associated with the object, and S/MIME and PGP/MIME can provide it.

Resources consumed by dialout are the next concern. Beyond the CPU cycles and disk that email uses, an offramp fax causes an outdial that often costs real money, so techniques for authorizing the sender are essential for gateways that need to manage that cost, and unsolicited bulk mail that causes an outdial is undesirable. There are no standard techniques for authorization using Internet protocols; typical solutions use simple authentication of the originator, or encryption-based data signing, and then check the identity against a private authorization table. Other common controls are source filtering, where the gateway checks the host or network the message came from, and originator authentication.

Confidential GSTN authorization information, such as a calling card authorization number, might be disclosed to the G3Fax recipient on the cover page, for example through parameters encoded in the address in the To or CC fields. Senders should be given a way of preventing such disclosure, but there are not yet standard mechanisms for protecting that information; out-of-band communication of the authorization information or encrypted data in special fields are the available non-standard techniques. Authorization usually needs to be tied to a specific sender and a specific message, to stop a replay attack in which an earlier authorization lets a later dial-out happen by a different and unauthorized sender. A harmless version of the same problem is an email recipient who replies to all the original recipients, including a fax recipient, so that the original sender's authorization causes the reply to be sent.

Sender accountability is the next point. In many countries there is a legal requirement that the sender be disclosed on a facsimile message, and email From addresses are trivial to fake, so using only the MAIL FROM or From header is not sufficient. Offramps should ensure the recipient is given contact information about the offramp in case of problems, and the G3Fax recipient should be given enough information to trace the originator, which might include the contents of the MAIL FROM, From, Sender and Reply-To headers, and the Message-ID and Received headers.

Message disclosure matters because users of fax devices expect a higher level of message privacy than mail without security enhancements gives, and that expectation should be preserved as far as possible; the usual mechanism for ensuring confidentiality is encryption. With non-private mailboxes, bounces usually go back to the sender rather than to a publicly accessible account or printer, but a fax bounce could go elsewhere, such as a local system administrator's account, a publicly accessible account, or an IFax printer. Traffic analysis is easier on the Internet than on the telephone network, and while encrypting the message does not prevent traffic analysis, channel security can help to frustrate such attempts.

Two kinds of encryption-based security support authentication and privacy. Channel security protects a message as it traverses internal networks or the Internet, using virtual private networks, encrypted tunnels or transport layer security, and also gives some protection against traffic analysis; IPsec and TLS are the protocols mentioned for this. Object security protects a message while it resides on, or is relayed through, an intermediate mail transfer agent, using message encryption to give end-to-end encryption, with PGP-MIME and S/MIME mentioned as the two protocols commonly used.
sections.plainLanguage: Joining mail and the telephone network raises questions that neither service has on its own. A mail address can be faked, so the sender of a fax may not be who the message says. Dialing out costs money, so a gateway needs some way to check who may send through it, and there is no standard way to do that. A calling card number can leak onto the fax cover page. And a fax is expected to be more private than an email, which plain mail does not deliver.

items.title: Onramp
items.text: Connects from the telephone facsimile to Internet mail. Its behaviour is out of scope.

items.title: Offramp
items.text: Connects from Internet mail to the telephone facsimile and performs the dial-out.

items.title: Serving many users
items.text: A gateway that behaves like a mail transfer agent, and should use SMTP.

items.title: Serving one user
items.text: A gateway that behaves like a mail user agent, and may use a mailbox access protocol.

viz.caption: THE EXTRA THREADS THAT COME WITH JOINING THE TWO SERVICES

items.title: Spoofed sender
items.text: The real sender may not be the one named in the headers or in the envelope.

items.title: Cost of dial-out
items.text: A fax costs money to send, so bulk mail that causes a dial-out is a problem.

items.title: Confidential details on the cover page
items.text: A calling card number may be shown to the fax recipient; senders should be able to prevent that.

items.title: Sender accountability
items.text: Many countries require the sender to be disclosed on a fax, and email addresses are easy to fake.

items.title: Message disclosure
items.text: Fax users expect more privacy than plain mail gives them.

items.title: Traffic analysis
items.text: It is easier to see who is sending to whom on the Internet than on the telephone network.
